quarterly_data.signal: Fiscal Q1 2026 results (CEO/CFO): record total revenues of $12.3 billion and record non-GAAP EPS of $3.50, with non-GAAP EPS at the high end of guidance. QCT posted record revenues of $10.6 billion driven by flagship handsets: QCT handset revenues were a record $7.8 billion, QCT IoT revenues were $1.7 billion (up 9% year-over-year) and QCT Automotive was another record at $1.1 billion (up 15%). QCT EBT margin of 31% came in line with expectations, exceeding the long-term 30% target. Licensing (QTL) revenues were $1.6 billion, and Qualcomm returned $3.6 billion to stockholders.
quarterly_data.figure: revenues $12.3 billion (record); non-GAAP EPS $3.50; QCT revenues $10.6 billion; QCT handset $7.8 billion; QCT Automotive $1.1 billion (up 15%); QCT EBT margin 31%

quarterly_data.signal: Fiscal Q2 2026 guidance (CFO), which reflects reduced chipset orders from handset OEMs, especially in China, that cut build plans and channel inventory because of memory: revenues of $10.2 billion to $11 billion and non-GAAP EPS of $2.45 to $2.65. QCT revenues are guided to $8.8 billion to $9.4 billion, with QCT handset revenues of approximately $6 billion 'as a result of the impact of memory constraints'. QTL is guided to $1.2 billion to $1.4 billion. QCT IoT should grow by a low-teens percentage year-over-year, and QCT Automotive growth should accelerate to greater than 35%. Non-GAAP operating expenses should be approximately $2.6 billion, reflecting calendar-year resets, employee-related costs and the completed AlphaWave acquisition. Gross margin is expected to be largely in line with the December quarter. The CFO did not guide past Q2 but said to think of March as 'a reasonable way to model June as well', and that for the full year 'we have a negative bias on units' given supply. Qualcomm expects QCT handset revenues to return to their prior run rate and growth trajectory once memory conditions normalize.
quarterly_data.figure: Q2 revenues $10.2 billion to $11 billion; QCT $8.8 billion to $9.4 billion; QCT handset approximately $6 billion; Automotive growth greater than 35%; non-GAAP opex approximately $2.6 billion

quarterly_data.signal: CALL-ONLY / QUALCOMM WARNS THAT HBM IS CROWDING OUT HANDSET DRAM. CEO Cristiano Amon: 'As memory suppliers redirect manufacturing capacity to HBM to meet AI data center demand, the resulting industry-wide memory shortage and price increases are likely to define the overall scale of the handset industry through the fiscal year.' In Q&A he called the March-quarter handset weakness '100% related to memory'. Handset demand and sell-through are strong, but 'DRAM availability for consumer electronics, especially handsets, is actually down bias on a year-over-year because of the prioritization of HBM for data centers', so customers are cutting builds to fit the memory they can get. Management added that 'memory vendors have prioritized the build out of HBM' and that memory supply for consumer electronics has been below demand, with similar commentary now coming from gaming consoles and other consumer devices. On duration: 'We can't really predict if this will continue for 2027 or 2028'. The answer depends on planned capacity build-outs and how fast the data-center trend accelerates. The issue 'is not just the price. The issue is just availability'. OEMs are expected to prioritize the premium and high tiers, and automotive is 'a little bit less sensitive to memory price increases'.
quarterly_data.figure: handset weakness '100% related to memory'; fiscal-year handset market size set by DRAM availability

quarterly_data.signal: Supply-side position (management): 'For handsets, we don't buy memory'. Apart from some memory that gets stacked, customers buy most memory directly. Qualcomm says it is 'probably among the first to be qualified with every memory provider', including CXMT and other smaller companies. Its platforms have a multi-generation memory controller that works with both newer and older memory, so 'we're going to work with whatever is available'. On foundry supply: 'leading nodes are constrained on the wafer side as well. But we have great relationships with our suppliers, and so we're confident that we'll have enough wafers to address the demand.'

Data-center status (CEO): 'the only public customer announced today is Humane that is progressing well. We have started shipping.' (name as printed in the transcript). Qualcomm has been working with that customer and ISVs on third-party workloads. Amon added that a company of Qualcomm's size would be expected to be in conversations with some of the largest hyperscalers and cloud service providers, and that broad engagements are giving very positive feedback. Execution runs on two fronts: CPU, where a RISC-V CPU now sits alongside the Arm-compatible Orion, and 'AI250 with our new memory architecture'. Qualcomm says it does 'very, very well in certain workloads such as decode' because of its different approach to compute and memory, and that 'the transaction of Grok' (name as printed; an analyst later asked 'What's happened since Grok? With NVIDIA?') 'kind of validates' specialized hardware in a disaggregated data center, 'versus just a GPU that would do everything'. On timing: 'We still restate that we expect 2027 to start showing in revenues'. The CFO called data center 'a multibillion revenue opportunity in a couple of years'. Amon said Qualcomm spans 'sub-five watts to now all the way to 500 watts' and focuses on inference, especially the disaggregated data center. In decode applications he believes Qualcomm is 'incredibly competitive' on power consumption, overall TCO, compute density and memory density. Roadmap details were deferred to the next investor event.
quarterly_data.figure: data-center revenue expected to start showing in 2027; 'multibillion revenue opportunity in a couple of years'

quarterly_data.signal: Data-center connectivity (CEO): 'In fiscal Q1, we completed the Alpha Wave SEMI acquisition, adding high-speed wire connectivity technology to further strengthen our platforms.' The CFO said the completed AlphaWave acquisition, made 'to further strengthen our platforms for next-generation AI data centers', is one reason non-GAAP opex rises sequentially. Under the CFO's opex framework, investment in mature businesses is reduced to fund diversification priorities, and acquisitions including Alphawave are separately 'driving incremental expense and investment in data center'.
quarterly_data.figure: Alphawave (Alpha Wave SEMI) acquisition completed in fiscal Q1

players.product: Dragonfly C1000 Arm-based AI data-center CPU

quarterly_data.signal: Server-CPU roadmap adds RISC-V (CEO): 'We added a RISC V CPU now to our roadmap in addition to Orion, which is ARM compatible.' Alongside the fiscal Q1 Alphawave close, Qualcomm 'also acquired Ventana Micro Systems', 'reinforcing our leadership and commitment to expanding the RISC V standard in the ecosystem, and development of our high-performance RISC V CPU for data center workloads'. Amon reported 'positive feedback on our CPU and innovative AI processing and memory architecture for next-generation inferencing data centers' as Qualcomm engages with leading hyperscalers, cloud service providers, sovereign AI projects and other partners. A roadmap update was promised for the next investor event.
